questions.q: Which long bone of the upper limb is the first bone to begin ossifying in the fetus and ossifies partly via intramembranous ossification?
questions.explain: The clavicle begins ossifying in the fifth to sixth fetal week, primarily through intramembranous ossification of its medial and lateral shaft before endochondral ossification contributes to its ends. Most other long bones ossify purely by endochondral ossification.

open.q: Which upper limb bone is the first to begin ossifying in utero and ossifies largely by intramembranous ossification?

questions.q: On which surface of the scapula is the deep subscapular fossa located?
questions.explain: The costal (anterior) surface of the scapula faces the thoracic cage and contains the concave subscapular fossa, which serves as the origin of subscapularis. The scapular spine divides the posterior surface into supraspinous and infraspinous fossae.

open.q: Which surface of the scapula contains the subscapular fossa?

questions.q: Which groove on the humeral shaft lodges the radial nerve and profunda brachii artery as they wind around the back of the humerus?
questions.explain: The radial (spiral) groove runs obliquely across the posterior surface of the humerus between the lateral and medial heads of triceps brachii, carrying the radial nerve and profunda brachii artery. Mid-shaft humeral fractures can injure these structures.

open.q: Which groove on the posterior humerus contains the radial nerve and profunda brachii artery?

questions.q: Which prominent bony feature at the proximal end of the ulna forms the point of the elbow and receives the triceps brachii tendon?
questions.explain: The olecranon is the large proximal projection of the ulna that fits into the olecranon fossa of the humerus during elbow extension and serves as the insertion site for triceps brachii. The coronoid process lies anteriorly below the trochlear notch.

open.q: Which proximal ulnar projection forms the prominence of the elbow and receives triceps brachii?

questions.q: Which carpal bone of the proximal row is most commonly fractured after a fall onto an outstretched hand, risking avascular necrosis of its proximal pole?
questions.explain: The scaphoid lies across both proximal and distal carpal rows and is vulnerable to fracture on a fall onto an outstretched hand (FOOSH). Its retrograde blood supply enters distally, making the proximal pole prone to avascular necrosis or non-union.

open.q: Which carpal bone is most frequently fractured after a fall onto an outstretched hand and can develop proximal pole avascular necrosis?

questions.q: Why does a fracture of the surgical neck of the humerus place the axillary nerve at risk?
options: The axillary nerve passes through the olecranon fossa
The axillary nerve winds around the surgical neck with the posterior circumflex humeral artery
The axillary nerve lies within the carpal tunnel
The axillary nerve pierces the medial epicondyle
questions.explain: After passing through the quadrangular space, the axillary nerve wraps posteriorly around the surgical neck of the humerus alongside the posterior circumflex humeral artery. Surgical neck fractures or anterior shoulder dislocations can injure it.

open.q: Why can a fracture of the surgical neck of the humerus injure the axillary nerve?
accept: the axillary nerve winds closely around the surgical neck
it courses directly against the surgical neck
the nerve wraps around the surgical neck with the posterior circumflex humeral artery
it lies in close anatomical contact with the surgical neck

questions.q: Which bony landmark on the medial side of the distal humerus is directly related to the ulnar nerve behind the elbow?
questions.explain: The ulnar nerve passes posterior to the medial epicondyle of the humerus in the cubital tunnel/ulnar groove, making it palpable and susceptible to injury at the elbow or in medial epicondyle fractures.

open.q: Behind which humeral prominence does the ulnar nerve pass at the elbow?

questions.q: Which muscle forms the bulk of the anterior chest wall and adducts and medially rotates the humerus?
questions.explain: Pectoralis major is a large fan-shaped muscle of the anterior chest wall that adducts, medially rotates, and (via its clavicular head) flexes the humerus. Pectoralis minor lies deep to it and attaches to the coracoid process.

open.q: Which large anterior chest muscle adducts and medially rotates the humerus?

questions.q: Damage to the long thoracic nerve during axillary surgery leads to paralysis of serratus anterior and causes which characteristic clinical sign?
questions.explain: Serratus anterior holds the medial border of the scapula against the thoracic wall and protracts/rotates the scapula during overhead arm elevation. Paralysis from long thoracic nerve injury causes winging of the scapula, especially when pushing forward or raising the arm.

open.q: What clinical sign results from paralysis of serratus anterior due to long thoracic nerve injury?

questions.q: Approximately what proportion of lymph from the mammary gland (breast) drains into the axillary lymph nodes?
options: None, it drains only to popliteal nodes
questions.explain: Roughly 75% of breast lymph drains toward the axillary lymph nodes (especially from the lateral quadrants), while much of the remainder drains to parasternal (internal thoracic) nodes. Axillary nodes are a key route for breast cancer spread and staging.

open.q: Approximately what percentage of lymphatic drainage from the breast goes to the axillary lymph nodes?

questions.q: Which structure forms the anterior wall of the axilla?
options: Subscapularis, teres major, and latissimus dorsi
First rib, outer border of rib 1, and clavicle
questions.explain: The anterior axillary wall is formed primarily by pectoralis major and pectoralis minor (along with clavipectoral fascia). The posterior wall is formed by subscapularis, teres major, and latissimus dorsi.

open.q: Which muscles form the anterior wall of the axilla?

questions.q: Which roots of the spinal nerves typically form the brachial plexus?
questions.explain: The brachial plexus is formed by the anterior rami of C5, C6, C7, C8, and T1, supplying motor and sensory innervation to the upper limb. C1 to C4 form the cervical plexus.

open.q: Which spinal nerve roots form the brachial plexus?

questions.q: Which terminal branch of the brachial plexus arises from the lateral and medial cords and supplies most flexors of the forearm and intrinsic muscles of the thenar eminence?
questions.explain: The median nerve is formed by contributions from the lateral and medial cords (C5 to T1) and innervates most anterior forearm flexors (except flexor carpi ulnaris and medial flexor digitorum profundus) plus the thenar muscles and lateral two lumbricals.

open.q: Which major nerve of the upper limb is formed by the lateral and medial cords and supplies most forearm flexors and thenar muscles?

questions.q: A newborn delivered with difficult shoulder dystocia has traction injury to the upper trunk (C5 to C6) of the brachial plexus, resulting in an adducted, medially rotated arm and extended pronated forearm. What is this pattern called?
questions.explain: Erb-Duchenne palsy involves C5 to C6 (upper trunk) injury, paralyzing abductors/lateral rotators of the shoulder (deltoid, supraspinatus) and elbow flexors/supinators (biceps, brachialis, brachioradialis), giving the classic waiter's tip posture. Klumpke palsy affects C8 to T1 (lower trunk).

open.q: What palsy results from upper brachial plexus (C5 to C6) injury and produces an adducted, medially rotated arm with extended forearm?

questions.q: Which cord of the brachial plexus gives rise to the axillary nerve and radial nerve?
questions.explain: The posterior cord of the brachial plexus divides into the axillary nerve (C5 to C6) and the radial nerve (C5 to T1), supplying posterior compartment muscles of the arm and forearm along with associated skin.

open.q: From which cord of the brachial plexus do the axillary and radial nerves originate?

questions.q: Which four muscles constitute the rotator cuff (SITS) of the shoulder joint?
options: Deltoid, teres major, latissimus dorsi, and pectoralis major
Supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, and subscapularis
Coracobrachialis, biceps brachii, brachialis, and triceps brachii
Rhomboid major, rhomboid minor, levator scapulae, and trapezius
questions.explain: The rotator cuff comprises supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, and subscapularis, whose tendons blend with the fibrous capsule of the glenohumeral joint to dynamically stabilize the humeral head.

open.q: Which four muscles form the rotator cuff of the shoulder?
accept: supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, and subscapularis

questions.q: Which rotator cuff muscle is primarily responsible for initiating abduction of the arm at the glenohumeral joint (roughly the first 15 degrees)?
questions.explain: Supraspinatus (supplied by the suprascapular nerve) initiates shoulder abduction for the first ~15 degrees before the deltoid gains mechanical advantage. Subscapularis medially rotates, while infraspinatus and teres minor laterally rotate.

open.q: Which rotator cuff muscle initiates abduction of the arm at the shoulder joint?

questions.q: Which structures pass through the quadrangular space of the posterior scapular/axillary region?
options: Radial nerve and profunda brachii artery
Suprascapular nerve and transverse cervical artery
Axillary nerve and posterior circumflex humeral artery
questions.explain: The quadrangular space is bounded by teres minor superiorly, teres major inferiorly, long head of triceps medially, and surgical neck of the humerus laterally, transmitting the axillary nerve and posterior circumflex humeral artery.

open.q: Which nerve and artery pass through the quadrangular space?
accept: axillary nerve and posterior circumflex humeral artery
axillary nerve with posterior circumflex humeral artery

questions.q: Which nerve innervates the three muscles of the anterior (flexor) compartment of the arm: biceps brachii, brachialis, and coracobrachialis?
questions.explain: The musculocutaneous nerve (C5 to C7) pierces coracobrachialis and supplies coracobrachialis, biceps brachii, and brachialis in the anterior arm compartment, continuing distally as the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm.

open.q: Which nerve supplies the muscles of the anterior compartment of the arm?

questions.q: Why does brachialis remain an effective elbow flexor even when the forearm is pronated, whereas biceps brachii loses much of its supination-linked mechanical advantage?
options: Brachialis inserts onto the radius and supinates the forearm
Brachialis inserts onto the ulna, so elbow flexion is maintained regardless of forearm rotation
Brachialis is supplied by the femoral nerve
Biceps brachii inserts onto the ulna and loses its flexion action in pronation
questions.explain: Brachialis crosses only the elbow joint and inserts onto the ulna, flexing the elbow efficiently in any forearm position. Biceps brachii inserts onto the radial tuberosity and acts as both a powerful supinator of a flexed forearm and an elbow flexor.

open.q: Why does brachialis flex the elbow effectively regardless of forearm rotation?
accept: it inserts onto the ulna rather than the rotating radius
its ulnar insertion is unaffected by pronation or supination
it attaches to the ulna across the elbow

questions.q: Which muscle forms the sole or primary muscle of the posterior (extensor) compartment of the arm and is supplied by the radial nerve?
questions.explain: Triceps brachii (long, lateral, and medial heads) occupies the posterior compartment of the arm and extends the elbow, receiving innervation from the radial nerve.

open.q: Which muscle occupies the posterior compartment of the arm and extends the elbow?

questions.q: From lateral to medial, what are the main neurovascular contents within the cubital fossa?
options: Ulnar nerve, brachial artery, and radial nerve
Median nerve, radial nerve, and ulnar artery
Brachial vein, ulnar artery, and musculocutaneous nerve
Radial nerve, biceps tendon, brachial artery, and median nerve
questions.explain: Within the cubital fossa (bounded superiorly by an interepicondylar line, laterally by brachioradialis, and medially by pronator teres), the structures from lateral to medial are the radial nerve (deep/lateral), tendon of biceps brachii, brachial artery, and median nerve.

open.q: List the main structures in the cubital fossa from lateral to medial.
accept: radial nerve, biceps tendon, brachial artery, and median nerve
radial nerve, tendon of biceps brachii, brachial artery, median nerve

questions.q: Why is the median cubital vein in the superficial fascia over the cubital fossa commonly chosen for venipuncture?
options: It is superficial and accessible; the bicipital aponeurosis helps protect the deeper brachial artery and median nerve
It lies within the brachial artery and provides an arterial sample
It is deep to the biceps tendon and difficult to compress
It has no communications with the deep venous system
questions.explain: The median cubital vein bridges the cephalic and basilic veins superficially over the cubital fossa, and the underlying bicipital aponeurosis provides a protective barrier between it and the deeper brachial artery and median nerve.

open.q: Why is the median cubital vein frequently used for venipuncture at the elbow?
accept: it is superficial and separated from the brachial artery and median nerve by the bicipital aponeurosis
superficial location with bicipital aponeurosis protecting deeper vessels and nerve
accessible superficial position over the bicipital aponeurosis
superficial vein shielded from deeper artery and nerve by the bicipital aponeurosis

questions.q: A patient has a mid-shaft fracture of the humerus and presents with inability to extend the wrist and metacarpophalangeal joints (wrist drop) with sensory loss over the dorsolateral hand. Which nerve is injured?
questions.explain: Radial nerve injury at or above the elbow paralyzes posterior forearm extensors of the wrist and fingers, producing wrist drop, and causes sensory loss over the dorsum of the hand/first web space.

open.q: Injury to which nerve causes wrist drop and loss of extension at the wrist and fingers?

questions.q: Which nerve innervates flexor carpi ulnaris and the medial half of flexor digitorum profundus in the anterior forearm?
questions.explain: While most anterior forearm flexors are innervated by the median nerve, flexor carpi ulnaris and the ulnar (medial) half of flexor digitorum profundus are supplied by the ulnar nerve.

open.q: Which nerve innervates flexor carpi ulnaris and the medial half of flexor digitorum profundus?

questions.q: Which muscle in the anterior forearm acts as a pronator of the forearm and arises from both a humeral head and an ulnar head?
questions.explain: Pronator teres has humeral and ulnar heads (with the median nerve passing between them) and inserts onto the lateral radius to pronate and weakly flex the forearm.

open.q: Which forearm muscle has humeral and ulnar heads and pronates the forearm?

questions.q: Which nerve branch supplies motor innervation to the deep extensor muscles of the posterior forearm (such as extensor digitorum and extensor pollicis longus) after passing through supinator?
questions.explain: The posterior interosseous nerve is the motor continuation of the deep branch of the radial nerve after it passes through supinator, innervating posterior forearm extensors without carrying cutaneous sensory fibers to the hand.

open.q: Which nerve supplies the posterior forearm extensor muscles after passing through supinator?

questions.q: Which nerve branch in the anterior forearm innervates flexor pollicis longus, pronator quadratus, and the lateral half of flexor digitorum profundus?
questions.explain: The anterior interosseous nerve is a purely motor branch of the median nerve in the forearm that runs along the anterior interosseous membrane to supply flexor pollicis longus, pronator quadratus, and the lateral half of flexor digitorum profundus.

open.q: Which branch of the median nerve supplies flexor pollicis longus and pronator quadratus?

questions.q: A patient cannot flex the interphalangeal joint of the thumb or the distal interphalangeal joint of the index finger when asked to make an OK sign, yet sensation in the median nerve palm is intact. Which nerve is affected?
questions.explain: Anterior interosseous nerve lesion selectively weakens flexor pollicis longus (thumb IP flexion) and lateral flexor digitorum profundus (index DIP flexion) plus pronator quadratus, sparing palmar cutaneous sensation because the palmar cutaneous branch arises proximal to the carpal tunnel.

open.q: Loss of thumb interphalangeal and index distal interphalangeal flexion with spared palmar sensation points to a lesion of which nerve?

questions.q: Which muscle forms the lateral border of the cubital fossa and flexes the elbow most effectively when the forearm is in the mid-prone position?
questions.explain: Brachioradialis originates on the lateral supracondylar ridge of the humerus and inserts on the distal radius, forming the lateral boundary of the cubital fossa and acting as an elbow flexor in mid-pronation despite being innervated by the radial nerve.

open.q: Which radial-innervated muscle forms the lateral border of the cubital fossa and flexes the mid-prone forearm?

questions.q: What fibrous band bridges the radial and ulnar sides of the carpus anteriorly to convert the carpal arch into the carpal tunnel?
questions.explain: The flexor retinaculum spans from the scaphoid and trapezium laterally to the pisiform and hook of hamate medially, forming the roof of the carpal tunnel through which the median nerve and flexor tendons pass.

open.q: What structure forms the roof of the carpal tunnel across the anterior wrist?

questions.q: Why is palmar sensation over the thenar eminence typically preserved in classic carpal tunnel syndrome?
options: The thenar skin is supplied by the radial nerve
The palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve passes superficial to the flexor retinaculum
The ulnar nerve supplies the entire palmar surface of the thumb
The carpal tunnel contains no sensory fibers
questions.explain: The palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve branches off proximal to the wrist and travels superficial to the flexor retinaculum, bypassing compression inside the carpal tunnel and preserving sensation over the central/thenar palm.

open.q: Why does carpal tunnel syndrome usually spare sensation over the central/thenar palm?
accept: the palmar cutaneous branch runs superficial to the flexor retinaculum
palmar cutaneous branch bypasses the carpal tunnel
palmar cutaneous branch is superficial to the retinaculum
sensation is carried by a branch outside the carpal tunnel

questions.q: Which tendons pass through the carpal tunnel alongside the median nerve?
options: Extensor digitorum and extensor pollicis longus tendons
Flexor carpi ulnaris and palmaris longus tendons
Four FDS, four FDP and one FPL tendon
Abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis tendons
questions.explain: Nine flexor tendons—four of flexor digitorum superficialis, four of flexor digitorum profundus, and one of flexor pollicis longus—pass through the carpal tunnel together with the median nerve. Flexor carpi radialis has its own canal.

open.q: Which flexor tendons travel through the carpal tunnel with the median nerve?
accept: flexor digitorum superficialis, flexor digitorum profundus, and flexor pollicis longus

questions.q: Which artery can be palpated on the lateral anterior wrist just lateral to the tendon of flexor carpi radialis?
questions.explain: The radial artery lies superficially on the distal radius lateral to flexor carpi radialis tendon, making it the standard site for palpating the radial pulse and obtaining arterial blood gas or catheter access.

open.q: Which artery is palpated at the lateral wrist just lateral to flexor carpi radialis?

questions.q: Which two tendons form the lateral (radial) boundary of the anatomical snuffbox at the base of the thumb?
options: Abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis
Extensor pollicis longus and extensor indicis
Flexor carpi radialis and palmaris longus
Flexor carpi ulnaris and extensor carpi ulnaris
questions.explain: The anatomical snuffbox is bounded laterally by tendons of abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis, and medially by extensor pollicis longus. The radial artery crosses its floor, and the scaphoid lies deep in it.

open.q: Which two tendons form the lateral border of the anatomical snuffbox?
accept: abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis

questions.q: Which group of intrinsic hand muscles forms the fleshy prominence at the base of the thumb and enables opposition?
questions.explain: The thenar eminence comprises abductor pollicis brevis, opponens pollicis, and flexor pollicis brevis, enabling abduction, opposition, and flexion of the thumb; they are typically supplied by the recurrent branch of the median nerve.

open.q: Which group of hand muscles forms the thenar eminence at the base of the thumb?

questions.q: What are the actions of the palmar interossei of the hand relative to the axial line of the middle finger?
options: Adduct the digits toward the middle finger
questions.explain: Using the PAD and DAB mnemonic, palmar interossei (PAD) adduct the fingers toward the axis of the middle finger, while dorsal interossei (DAB) abduct the fingers away from that axis.

open.q: What movement do the palmar interossei produce in the fingers?

questions.q: Which nerve innervates the vast majority of intrinsic hand muscles, including the hypothenar muscles, interossei, adductor pollicis, and medial two lumbricals?
questions.explain: The ulnar nerve supplies the hypothenar muscles, all palmar and dorsal interossei, adductor pollicis, and the third and fourth (medial two) lumbricals. The median nerve supplies the thenar muscles and first two (lateral two) lumbricals.

open.q: Which nerve supplies the interossei, hypothenar muscles, adductor pollicis, and medial two lumbricals?

questions.q: How do the lumbrical muscles of the hand affect joint positions of the fingers?
options: They flex the metacarpophalangeal joints while extending the interphalangeal joints
They extend the metacarpophalangeal joints while flexing the interphalangeal joints
They insert exclusively onto the pisiform
questions.explain: Lumbricals arise from flexor digitorum profundus tendons and insert into the extensor expansions on the dorsal aspect of the proximal phalanges, enabling flexion at the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints combined with extension at the interphalangeal (IP) joints.

open.q: What combined movement do the lumbricals produce at the finger joints?
accept: flexion at metacarpophalangeal joints and extension at interphalangeal joints
flex mcp joints and extend ip joints

questions.q: A patient has a lesion of the ulnar nerve at the elbow or wrist and cannot adduct the little finger or adduct the thumb firmly against the index finger (Froment sign). Which muscle primarily adducts the thumb?
questions.explain: Adductor pollicis adducts the thumb toward the palm/index finger and is innervated by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve. Paralysis causes weak pinch/adduction, often compensated by flexor pollicis longus (Froment sign).

open.q: Which ulnar-innervated muscle adducts the thumb and is tested when checking for Froment sign?

questions.q: Which joint is the only synovial articulation between the axial skeleton and the upper limb girdle?
questions.explain: The sternoclavicular joint connects the sternal end of the clavicle, the manubrium of the sternum, and the first costal cartilage, serving as the sole synovial linkage between the upper limb skeleton and axial skeleton.

open.q: Which joint is the sole synovial connection between the upper limb girdle and the axial skeleton?

questions.q: Which fibrocartilaginous structure deepens the shallow glenoid cavity of the scapula at the shoulder joint?
questions.explain: The glenoid labrum is a fibrocartilaginous rim attached around the margin of the glenoid cavity that deepens the socket slightly and increases contact area with the humeral head.

open.q: What fibrocartilaginous rim deepens the glenoid cavity of the shoulder joint?

questions.q: What is the function of the annular ligament of the radius at the proximal radioulnar joint?
options: It holds the radial head against the radial notch while permitting pronation and supination
It attaches the ulna to the humeral trochlea during elbow extension
It prevents all rotation at the proximal radioulnar joint
It connects the clavicle to the coracoid process
questions.explain: The annular ligament forms a strong fibrous collar around the head of the radius attached to the ulna, keeping the radial head within the radial notch during pronation and supination. In young children, traction can pull the radial head partially out of it (pulled elbow).

open.q: How does the annular ligament stabilize the head of the radius during forearm rotation?
accept: it encircles the radial head against the radial notch of the ulna while permitting rotation
holds the head of the radius in the radial notch so it can rotate
collars the radial head against the ulna
keeps the radial head in place during pronation and supination

questions.q: Which movement occurs at the radioulnar joints when the palm turns anteriorly (from anatomical position/supination) or posteriorly?
questions.explain: The proximal and distal radioulnar joints allow the radius to pivot around the ulna, producing pronation (turning palm posteriorly/downward) and supination (turning palm anteriorly/upward).

open.q: Which movements of the forearm take place at the radioulnar joints?

questions.q: At which anatomical landmark does the subclavian artery become the axillary artery?
options: Lateral border of the first rib
questions.explain: The subclavian artery continues as the axillary artery at the lateral border of the first rib, and the axillary artery continues as the brachial artery at the inferior border of teres major.

open.q: At which landmark does the subclavian artery transition into the axillary artery?
accept: lateral border of the first rib

questions.q: Along which side of the upper limb does the cephalic vein ascend before piercing the clavipectoral fascia to drain into the axillary vein?
questions.explain: The cephalic vein arises from the lateral side of the dorsal venous network of the hand, ascends along the lateral/anterolateral forearm and arm in the deltopectoral groove, and pierces the clavipectoral fascia to join the axillary vein.

open.q: Along which aspect of the upper limb does the cephalic vein ascend before joining the axillary vein?

questions.q: Where does the basilic vein pierce the deep fascia of the arm to join the brachial veins and form the axillary vein?
options: Near the middle of the medial arm
questions.explain: The basilic vein ascends along the medial aspect of the forearm and lower arm superficially, then pierces the brachial fascia around mid-arm to join the brachial (vena comitans) veins and form the axillary vein.

open.q: Around which region of the arm does the basilic vein pierce the deep fascia?
accept: middle of the arm on the medial side

questions.q: Which arterial arch in the palm is formed primarily as the direct continuation of the ulnar artery anastomosing with the superficial palmar branch of the radial artery?
questions.explain: The superficial palmar arch lies deep to the palmar aponeurosis and is formed mainly by the ulnar artery with a contribution from the superficial palmar branch of the radial artery, giving off common palmar digital arteries.

open.q: Which palmar arterial arch is formed mainly by the ulnar artery?

questions.q: How is the deep palmar arch in the hand primarily formed?
options: By the radial artery anastomosing with the deep palmar branch of the ulnar artery
By the musculocutaneous and axillary arteries
By the thoracoacromial and suprascapular arteries
questions.explain: The deep palmar arch lies across the bases of the metacarpals and is formed primarily by the terminal radial artery joining the deep palmar branch of the ulnar artery, giving off princeps pollicis, radialis indicis, and palmar metacarpal arteries.

open.q: Which arteries join to form the deep palmar arch of the hand?
accept: radial artery and deep palmar branch of the ulnar artery
terminal radial artery with deep branch of ulnar artery

questions.q: A patient has a supracondylar fracture of the humerus with severe anterior displacement of the distal fragment, threatening the brachial artery and median nerve. What ischemic complication of the forearm can follow untreated brachial artery injury?
questions.explain: Ischemia and compartment swelling in the anterior forearm after brachial artery injury or supracondylar humeral fracture can cause muscle and nerve necrosis followed by fibrous shortening, known as Volkmann ischemic contracture.

open.q: What forearm contracture can result from untreated ischemia after brachial artery injury or supracondylar humeral fracture?

questions.q: Where does the clavicle most commonly fracture?
options: Junction of the middle and lateral thirds
questions.explain: The junction of the middle and lateral thirds is the weakest point, where the curvature changes and no ligaments or muscles reinforce the bone.

open.q: At what part of the clavicle does fracture most commonly occur?
accept: junction of middle and outer thirds

questions.q: Which carpal bone is most commonly fractured?
questions.explain: The scaphoid is most often fractured, typically after a fall on the outstretched hand, usually at the waist.

open.q: Which carpal bone is most commonly fractured?

questions.q: Fracture across the waist of the scaphoid is most likely to cause which complication?
options: Avascular necrosis of the proximal fragment
questions.explain: The scaphoid is supplied by branches of the radial artery that enter distally and run retrograde, so the proximal fragment can lose its blood supply.

open.q: What complication of a scaphoid waist fracture results from its retrograde blood supply?

questions.q: Which artery crosses the floor of the anatomical snuffbox?
questions.explain: The radial artery crosses the floor of the snuffbox, over the scaphoid and trapezium, and its pulsation can be felt there.

open.q: Which artery crosses the floor of the anatomical snuffbox?

questions.q: A fracture of the surgical neck of the humerus most commonly injures which nerve?
questions.explain: The axillary nerve wraps around the surgical neck with the posterior circumflex humeral artery. A midshaft fracture injures the radial nerve instead.

open.q: Which nerve is most commonly injured in a fracture of the surgical neck of the humerus?

questions.q: A fracture of the midshaft of the humerus in the radial groove most commonly injures which nerve?
questions.explain: The radial nerve lies against the humerus in the radial (spiral) groove with the profunda brachii artery.

open.q: Which nerve is most commonly injured in a midshaft humeral fracture at the spiral groove?

questions.q: In a child with a displaced supracondylar fracture of the humerus, which vessel and nerve are at greatest risk?
options: Profunda brachii artery and radial nerve
questions.explain: The brachial artery and median nerve (especially its anterior interosseous branch) lie in front of the distal humerus. Ischaemia can lead to Volkmann ischaemic contracture.

open.q: Which artery and nerve are at greatest risk in a displaced supracondylar fracture of the humerus in a child?
accept: brachial artery and anterior interosseous nerve

questions.q: Which nerve is at risk in a fracture or avulsion of the medial epicondyle of the humerus?
questions.explain: The ulnar nerve runs in a groove on the back of the medial epicondyle, where it is superficial and easily damaged.

open.q: Which nerve is at risk in a fracture of the medial epicondyle of the humerus?

questions.q: What is a Colles fracture?
options: Fracture of the distal radius with dorsal displacement of the distal fragment
Fracture of the distal radius with volar displacement of the distal fragment
Fracture of the ulnar styloid with lunate dislocation
questions.explain: Colles fracture is a transverse distal radial fracture with dorsal displacement, giving the dinner-fork deformity. It is common after a fall on the outstretched hand.

open.q: What is a Colles fracture?
accept: distal radius fracture with dorsal displacement
dorsally displaced fracture of distal radius

questions.q: Which eponym describes a distal radius fracture with volar (anterior) displacement of the distal fragment?
questions.explain: A Smith fracture is a reverse Colles fracture, usually from a fall on the back of the flexed hand.

open.q: What is the eponym for a distal radius fracture with volar displacement of the distal fragment?

questions.q: A Bennett fracture involves which part of the hand?
questions.explain: Bennett fracture is an intra-articular fracture-dislocation of the base of the first metacarpal. The neck of the fifth metacarpal is the boxer's fracture.

open.q: Which part of the hand is fractured in a Bennett fracture?

questions.q: A fracture of the hook of the hamate may injure which structure?
options: Superficial branch of the radial nerve
Deep branch of the ulnar nerve
questions.explain: The deep branch of the ulnar nerve curves around the hook of the hamate, so a fracture there can weaken the intrinsic hand muscles.

open.q: Which nerve may be injured in a fracture of the hook of the hamate?

questions.q: Which bone of the body is the first to begin ossification?
questions.explain: The clavicle begins to ossify first, at about 5 to 6 weeks, by intramembranous ossification. Its medial end is the last long-bone epiphysis to fuse.

open.q: Which bone is the first in the body to begin ossification?

questions.q: Winging of the scapula on pushing against a wall results from injury to which nerve?
questions.explain: The long thoracic nerve (C5-C7) supplies serratus anterior. Paralysis lets the medial border of the scapula lift away from the chest wall.

open.q: Winging of the scapula from paralysis of serratus anterior is caused by injury to which nerve?

questions.q: Injury to the spinal accessory nerve (CN XI) paralyses which muscle?
questions.explain: CN XI supplies sternocleidomastoid and trapezius. Injury causes a drooping shoulder and weak shoulder elevation.

open.q: Which muscle of the shoulder girdle is paralysed when the spinal accessory nerve is injured?

questions.q: The thoracodorsal nerve supplies which muscle?
questions.explain: The thoracodorsal nerve (C6-C8) from the posterior cord supplies latissimus dorsi. It is at risk during axillary lymph node dissection.

open.q: Which muscle is supplied by the thoracodorsal nerve?

questions.q: The dorsal scapular nerve supplies which muscles?
questions.explain: The dorsal scapular nerve (C5), from the roots of the plexus, supplies the rhomboids and contributes to levator scapulae.

open.q: Which muscles are supplied by the dorsal scapular nerve?

questions.q: Which muscle forms the medial boundary of the triangle of auscultation?
questions.explain: The triangle is bounded by trapezius medially, latissimus dorsi inferolaterally and the medial border of the scapula superolaterally. Rhomboid major forms its floor.

open.q: Which muscle forms the medial boundary of the triangle of auscultation?

questions.q: Which rotator cuff muscle is an internal (medial) rotator of the arm?
questions.explain: Subscapularis medially rotates the arm. Infraspinatus and teres minor are lateral rotators.

open.q: Which rotator cuff muscle medially rotates the arm?

questions.q: Which rotator cuff muscle inserts on the lesser tubercle of the humerus?
questions.explain: Subscapularis inserts on the lesser tubercle. The other three cuff muscles insert on the greater tubercle.

open.q: Which rotator cuff muscle inserts on the lesser tubercle of the humerus?

questions.q: Which rotator cuff tendon is most commonly torn?
questions.explain: The supraspinatus tendon passes under the acromion and is prone to impingement, wear and tearing.

open.q: Which rotator cuff tendon is most commonly torn?

questions.q: The suprascapular nerve supplies which pair of muscles?
questions.explain: The suprascapular nerve (C5-C6) from the upper trunk passes through the suprascapular notch and supplies both supraspinatus and infraspinatus.

open.q: Which two muscles does the suprascapular nerve supply?

questions.q: Which structures pass through the quadrangular space?
options: Radial nerve and profunda brachii artery
Axillary nerve and posterior circumflex humeral artery
questions.explain: The quadrangular space lies between teres minor, teres major, the long head of triceps and the humerus. It transmits the axillary nerve and the posterior circumflex humeral vessels.

open.q: What nerve and artery pass through the quadrangular space?
accept: axillary nerve with posterior circumflex humeral artery
axillary nerve and posterior circumflex humeral vessels

questions.q: The triangular space, bounded by teres minor, teres major and the long head of triceps, transmits which structure?
questions.explain: The circumflex scapular artery passes through the triangular space to join the scapular anastomosis. The radial nerve passes through the triangular interval below.

open.q: Which vessel passes through the triangular space bounded by teres minor, teres major and the long head of triceps?

questions.q: Which muscle divides the axillary artery into three parts?
questions.explain: Pectoralis minor crosses the artery, giving parts one (medial to it), two (behind it) and three (lateral to it).

open.q: Which muscle divides the axillary artery into three parts?

questions.q: Which is the largest branch of the axillary artery?
questions.explain: The subscapular artery arises from the third part and gives the circumflex scapular and thoracodorsal arteries.

open.q: What is the largest branch of the axillary artery?

questions.q: At what landmark does the axillary artery become the brachial artery?
options: Lateral border of the first rib
questions.explain: The axillary artery begins at the lateral border of the first rib and ends at the inferior border of teres major, where it becomes the brachial artery.

open.q: At what landmark does the axillary artery change its name to the brachial artery?

questions.q: Which superficial vein joins the brachial veins to form the axillary vein?
questions.explain: The axillary vein is formed at the lower border of teres major from the basilic vein and the brachial veins. The cephalic vein joins it higher up.

open.q: Which superficial vein of the arm joins the brachial veins to form the axillary vein?

questions.q: In which groove does the cephalic vein ascend before it pierces the clavipectoral fascia?
questions.explain: The cephalic vein runs in the deltopectoral groove and then pierces the clavipectoral fascia to enter the axillary vein.

open.q: Which groove does the cephalic vein ascend in before draining into the axillary vein?
accept: groove between deltoid and pectoralis major

questions.q: Which group of axillary lymph nodes receives most of the lymph from the upper limb?
questions.explain: Most lymphatics from the upper limb drain to the lateral nodes. Vessels along the cephalic vein go to the apical nodes.

open.q: Which group of axillary lymph nodes receives most of the lymph from the upper limb?

questions.q: The brachial plexus is formed by the ventral rami of which spinal nerves?
questions.explain: The plexus is formed by the ventral rami of C5-C8 and T1, with occasional contributions from C4 or T2.

open.q: The brachial plexus is formed by the ventral rami of which spinal nerves?
accept: C5, C6, C7, C8 and T1

questions.q: Which structures pass between the anterior and middle scalene muscles?
options: Subclavian artery and the trunks of the brachial plexus
Internal jugular vein and common carotid artery
questions.explain: The subclavian artery and the roots and trunks of the brachial plexus pass through the interscalene gap. The subclavian vein passes in front of anterior scalene.

open.q: Which artery and nerve plexus pass between the anterior and middle scalene muscles?
accept: subclavian artery and brachial plexus trunks
subclavian artery and brachial plexus roots
subclavian artery with roots and trunks of brachial plexus

questions.q: Which part of the brachial plexus is injured in Erb-Duchenne palsy?
questions.explain: Excessive increase in the angle between the neck and shoulder, for example in a difficult delivery or a fall on the shoulder, injures the upper trunk.

open.q: Which part of the brachial plexus is injured in Erb-Duchenne palsy?

questions.q: What is the characteristic limb posture in Erb-Duchenne palsy called?
questions.explain: The arm is adducted and medially rotated with the elbow extended and the forearm pronated, as if receiving a tip.

open.q: What is the characteristic limb posture in Erb-Duchenne palsy called?

questions.q: A man falls from a ladder and grabs a branch with his arm hyperabducted. He develops a claw hand and ptosis. Which part of the brachial plexus is injured?
questions.explain: Klumpke paralysis affects C8-T1, weakening the intrinsic hand muscles. Involvement of the T1 sympathetic fibres causes Horner syndrome with ptosis.

open.q: A man grabs a branch with his arm hyperabducted and develops a claw hand and ptosis. Which part of the brachial plexus is injured?

questions.q: The median nerve is formed by contributions from which cords of the brachial plexus?
questions.explain: The lateral root of the median nerve comes from the lateral cord and the medial root from the medial cord, forming a V around the axillary artery.

open.q: Which two cords of the brachial plexus contribute roots to the median nerve?

questions.q: Which cord of the brachial plexus gives rise to both the axillary and radial nerves?
questions.explain: The posterior cord gives the upper and lower subscapular, thoracodorsal, axillary and radial nerves.

open.q: Which cord of the brachial plexus gives rise to both the axillary and radial nerves?

questions.q: Which muscle of the arm is supplied by the musculocutaneous nerve?
questions.explain: The musculocutaneous nerve supplies the anterior compartment of the arm: coracobrachialis, biceps brachii and brachialis.

open.q: Name a muscle in the anterior compartment of the arm that is supplied by the musculocutaneous nerve.

questions.q: After injury to the musculocutaneous nerve in the arm, where is sensation lost?
options: Palmar surface of the little finger
questions.explain: The musculocutaneous nerve continues as the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm, which supplies the lateral forearm skin.

open.q: After injury to the musculocutaneous nerve in the arm, which area of skin loses sensation?
accept: area of the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm

questions.q: The biceps tendon reflex tests which spinal cord segments?
questions.explain: The biceps reflex is mediated by the musculocutaneous nerve at C5-C6. The triceps reflex tests C7-C8.

open.q: The biceps tendon (bicipital) myotatic reflex tests which spinal cord segments?

questions.q: The triceps tendon reflex tests which spinal cord segments?
questions.explain: The triceps reflex is mediated by the radial nerve at C7-C8.

open.q: The triceps tendon reflex tests which spinal cord segments?

questions.q: Which tendon runs within the capsule of the glenohumeral joint?
options: Tendon of the short head of biceps
Tendon of the long head of biceps
questions.explain: The tendon of the long head of biceps arises from the supraglenoid tubercle and passes through the joint cavity into the intertubercular sulcus, surrounded by a synovial sheath.

open.q: Which muscle tendon passes through the cavity of the shoulder joint?
accept: long head of biceps brachii tendon

questions.q: Which muscle is the most powerful supinator against resistance when the elbow is flexed?
questions.explain: Biceps is the strongest supinator when the forearm is flexed, as in turning a screwdriver. Supinator does most unresisted supination.

open.q: Which muscle is the most powerful supinator of the forearm against resistance with the elbow flexed?

questions.q: Which vessel accompanies the radial nerve in the radial groove of the humerus?
questions.explain: The profunda brachii (deep brachial) artery runs with the radial nerve between the heads of triceps in the groove.

open.q: Which artery accompanies the radial nerve in the radial groove of the humerus?

questions.q: What is the characteristic deformity of a radial nerve palsy?
questions.explain: Paralysis of the extensors of the wrist and fingers leaves the wrist flexed and unable to extend, giving wrist drop.

open.q: What is the characteristic deformity of a radial nerve palsy?

questions.q: A patient with a midshaft humeral fracture has wrist drop but can still extend the elbow. What explains this?
options: Branches to the triceps arise proximal to the radial groove, so they may be spared
Triceps is supplied by the axillary nerve
Anconeus fully replaces all triceps function
Triceps is supplied by the ulnar nerve
questions.explain: The branches to triceps arise in the axilla and proximal arm, so a lesion in the groove spares elbow extension.

open.q: A patient with a midshaft humeral fracture has wrist drop but can still extend the elbow. Why is triceps spared?
accept: triceps branches arise proximal to the groove
nerve to triceps leaves before the spiral groove
branches to triceps come off high in the axilla

questions.q: Which structure lies immediately medial to the biceps tendon in the cubital fossa?
questions.explain: From lateral to medial the contents are the biceps tendon, brachial artery and median nerve.

open.q: Which vessel lies immediately medial to the biceps tendon in the cubital fossa?

questions.q: Which vein is most commonly used for venepuncture in the cubital fossa?
questions.explain: The median cubital vein is large, superficial and relatively fixed, and it connects the cephalic and basilic veins.

open.q: Which vein is most commonly used for venepuncture in the cubital fossa?

questions.q: Which two muscles form the floor of the cubital fossa?
questions.explain: The floor is formed by brachialis and supinator. The roof includes the bicipital aponeurosis and deep fascia.

open.q: Which two muscles form the floor of the cubital fossa?

questions.q: At what level does the brachial artery divide into the radial and ulnar arteries?
questions.explain: The brachial artery ends at the apex of the cubital fossa, level with the neck of the radius.

open.q: At what bony level does the brachial artery divide into the radial and ulnar arteries?

questions.q: The median nerve passes between the two heads of which muscle in the forearm?
questions.explain: The median nerve passes between the humeral and ulnar heads of pronator teres. Compression here causes pronator syndrome.

open.q: The median nerve passes between the two heads of which forearm muscle?

questions.q: The ulnar nerve enters the forearm between the two heads of which muscle?
questions.explain: The humeral and ulnar heads of flexor carpi ulnaris bridge the cubital tunnel, which is a site of ulnar nerve compression.

open.q: The ulnar nerve enters the forearm between the two heads of which muscle?

questions.q: Which nerve is compressed in cubital tunnel syndrome?
questions.explain: The ulnar nerve is compressed in the cubital tunnel behind the medial epicondyle, causing paraesthesia of the medial one and a half fingers.

open.q: Which nerve is compressed in cubital tunnel syndrome?

questions.q: Which nerve winds around the radius through the supinator muscle?
options: Superficial branch of the radial nerve
Deep branch of the radial nerve
questions.explain: The deep branch of the radial nerve pierces supinator and continues as the posterior interosseous nerve, which is a motor nerve to the extensor compartment.

open.q: Which nerve passes through the supinator muscle to enter the posterior compartment of the forearm?

questions.q: Which nerve supplies the skin over the anatomical snuffbox and the lateral dorsum of the hand?
options: Lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm
Dorsal branch of the ulnar nerve
Superficial branch of the radial nerve
Palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve
questions.explain: The superficial branch of the radial nerve is purely sensory and supplies the lateral two thirds of the dorsum of the hand.

open.q: Which nerve supplies the skin over the anatomical snuffbox and the lateral dorsum of the hand?

questions.q: In lateral epicondylitis (tennis elbow), which muscle's tendon is most commonly involved?
questions.explain: Overuse strain at the common extensor origin most often involves extensor carpi radialis brevis.

open.q: In lateral epicondylitis (tennis elbow), which muscle's tendon is most commonly involved?

questions.q: What is the common name for medial epicondylitis?
questions.explain: Golfer's elbow is inflammation of the common flexor origin on the medial epicondyle. Student's elbow is olecranon bursitis.

open.q: What is the common name for medial epicondylitis?

questions.q: What is the injury in mallet (baseball) finger?
options: Rupture of the extensor tendon over the proximal interphalangeal joint
Avulsion of the extensor tendon from the base of the distal phalanx
questions.explain: A blow to the tip of the extended finger avulses the extensor tendon from the distal phalanx. The distal phalanx then stays flexed and cannot be actively extended.

open.q: What is the injury in mallet (baseball) finger?
accept: avulsion of extensor tendon at distal phalanx
extensor tendon rupture at the DIP joint
extensor digitorum tendon detached from distal phalanx

questions.q: Which muscle pulls the fractured proximal fragment of the olecranon upward?
questions.explain: Triceps inserts on the olecranon. In a transverse fracture its pull displaces the proximal fragment away from the shaft.

open.q: Which muscle pulls the fractured proximal fragment of the olecranon away from the shaft?

questions.q: At the wrist, the radial pulse is palpated lateral to the tendon of which muscle?
questions.explain: The radial artery lies lateral to the flexor carpi radialis tendon and rests on the distal radius, where it is easy to feel.

open.q: At the wrist, the radial pulse is palpated lateral to the tendon of which muscle?

questions.q: Which forearm flexor is absent in about 14% of people and is commonly used as a tendon graft?
questions.explain: Palmaris longus is absent in some people without functional loss. Its tendon is often used for grafts.

open.q: Which forearm flexor muscle is absent in some people and is commonly used as a tendon graft?

questions.q: Which muscle is supplied by the anterior interosseous nerve?
questions.explain: The anterior interosseous nerve, from the median nerve, supplies flexor pollicis longus, the lateral half of flexor digitorum profundus and pronator quadratus.

open.q: Name a forearm muscle supplied by the anterior interosseous nerve that pronates the forearm.

questions.q: Which part of flexor digitorum profundus is supplied by the ulnar nerve?
options: Only the tendon to the index finger
questions.explain: The ulnar nerve supplies the medial half of FDP to the ring and little fingers. The lateral half is supplied by the anterior interosseous nerve.

open.q: Which part of flexor digitorum profundus is supplied by the ulnar nerve?

questions.q: Which forearm flexor muscle is supplied entirely by the ulnar nerve?
questions.explain: Flexor carpi ulnaris is the only forearm muscle supplied wholly by the ulnar nerve. All the other forearm flexors are supplied by the median nerve, except the medial half of FDP.

open.q: Which forearm flexor muscle is supplied entirely by the ulnar nerve?

questions.q: A woman reports night-time tingling of the thumb, index and middle fingers and weakness of the thenar muscles. Which nerve is compressed at the wrist?
questions.explain: This is carpal tunnel syndrome. The median nerve is compressed under the flexor retinaculum.

open.q: A woman reports night-time tingling of the thumb, index and middle fingers and weakness of the thenar muscles. Which nerve is compressed at the wrist?
accept: median nerve in the carpal tunnel

questions.q: Besides the tendons of flexor digitorum superficialis and profundus, which tendon passes through the carpal tunnel?
questions.explain: The carpal tunnel contains nine tendons and the median nerve. Palmaris longus lies superficial to the retinaculum, and flexor carpi radialis has its own sheath.

open.q: Besides the tendons of flexor digitorum superficialis and profundus, which long flexor tendon passes through the carpal tunnel?

questions.q: Why is sensation over the thenar eminence preserved in carpal tunnel syndrome?
options: The palmar cutaneous branch leaves the median nerve proximal to the tunnel and passes superficial to the retinaculum
The thenar skin is supplied by the ulnar nerve
The recurrent motor branch supplies the skin of the thenar eminence
The radial nerve supplies the thenar skin
questions.explain: The palmar cutaneous branch leaves the median nerve in the forearm and passes over the retinaculum, so it is not compressed.

open.q: Why is sensation over the thenar eminence preserved in carpal tunnel syndrome?
accept: palmar cutaneous branch passes superficial to the flexor retinaculum
palmar cutaneous branch arises proximal to the carpal tunnel
palmar branch of median nerve bypasses the tunnel

questions.q: Which thenar muscle is supplied by the recurrent (thenar) branch of the median nerve?
questions.explain: The recurrent branch supplies abductor pollicis brevis, opponens pollicis and the superficial head of flexor pollicis brevis. Adductor pollicis is supplied by the ulnar nerve.

open.q: Name a thenar muscle supplied by the recurrent branch of the median nerve that abducts the thumb.

questions.q: In an ulnar nerve injury, claw hand is most marked in which fingers?
questions.explain: The ulnar nerve supplies the medial two lumbricals. Their paralysis leaves the ring and little fingers hyperextended at the MCP joints and flexed at the IP joints.

open.q: In an ulnar nerve injury, claw hand is most marked in which fingers?

questions.q: Froment's sign tests the function of which muscle?
questions.explain: In ulnar nerve palsy, adductor pollicis cannot hold a sheet of paper, so flexor pollicis longus (median nerve) substitutes, flexing the thumb tip.

open.q: Froment's sign tests the function of which thumb muscle?

questions.q: Why is claw hand less marked in an ulnar nerve injury at the elbow than at the wrist?
options: The medial half of FDP is also paralysed, so distal phalanx flexion is lost
The lumbricals to the ring and little fingers keep working
questions.explain: A high lesion paralyses the medial half of flexor digitorum profundus as well, so the distal phalanges cannot flex and the clawing is less obvious (the ulnar paradox).

open.q: Why is claw hand less marked in an ulnar nerve injury at the elbow than at the wrist?
accept: FDP to digits 4 and 5 is paralysed
medial half of flexor digitorum profundus is paralysed

questions.q: In a median nerve lesion at the elbow, the index and middle fingers stay extended when the patient tries to make a fist. What is this sign called?
questions.explain: Loss of the median-supplied long flexors of digits 2 and 3 produces the hand of benediction. Ape hand refers to thenar wasting with a flattened thumb.

open.q: In a median nerve lesion at the elbow, the index and middle fingers stay extended when the patient tries to make a fist. What is this sign called?

questions.q: Which nerve supplies the hypothenar muscles?
options: Deep branch of the ulnar nerve
Superficial branch of the radial nerve
Recurrent branch of the median nerve
questions.explain: The deep branch of the ulnar nerve supplies the hypothenar muscles, the interossei, the adductor pollicis and the medial two lumbricals.

open.q: Which nerve supplies the hypothenar muscles?

questions.q: Which muscles abduct the fingers at the metacarpophalangeal joints?
questions.explain: Remember DAB and PAD: dorsal interossei abduct the fingers and palmar interossei adduct them.

open.q: Which muscles abduct the fingers at the metacarpophalangeal joints?

questions.q: Which muscles flex the metacarpophalangeal joints and extend the interphalangeal joints?
questions.explain: The lumbricals and interossei insert into the extensor expansions, so they flex the MCP joints and extend the PIP and DIP joints.

open.q: Which intrinsic hand muscles flex the metacarpophalangeal joints and extend the interphalangeal joints?

questions.q: Which nerve supplies the first and second lumbricals?
questions.explain: The lateral two lumbricals are supplied by the median nerve and the medial two by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve.

open.q: Which nerve supplies the first and second lumbricals?

questions.q: The superficial palmar arch is mainly formed by which artery?
questions.explain: The superficial palmar arch is the direct continuation of the ulnar artery, completed laterally by the superficial palmar branch of the radial artery.

open.q: The superficial palmar arch is mainly formed by which artery?

questions.q: The deep palmar arch is mainly formed by which artery?
questions.explain: The deep palmar arch is the direct continuation of the radial artery, completed medially by the deep branch of the ulnar artery.

open.q: The deep palmar arch is mainly formed by which artery?

questions.q: The Allen test is used to assess what?
options: Patency of the ulnar artery and collateral flow through the palmar arches
questions.explain: After compressing both wrist arteries and releasing one, return of colour shows that the released artery and palmar arches are patent.

open.q: What is the Allen test used to assess?
accept: patency of the radial and ulnar arteries
adequacy of palmar arch blood flow

questions.q: Dupuytren contracture is progressive fibrosis of which structure?
questions.explain: Fibrosis of the palmar aponeurosis draws the ring and little fingers into flexion.

open.q: Dupuytren contracture is progressive fibrosis of which structure of the hand?

questions.q: Tenosynovitis of the flexor sheath of which finger can spread to the palm through the ulnar bursa?
questions.explain: The sheath of the little finger is usually continuous with the common flexor sheath (ulnar bursa). Infection can spread through it to the midpalmar space.

open.q: Tenosynovitis of the flexor sheath of which finger can spread to the palm through the ulnar bursa?

questions.q: The radial bursa encloses the tendon of which muscle?
options: Flexor digitorum profundus to the index finger
questions.explain: The radial bursa is the synovial sheath of flexor pollicis longus and extends from the wrist to the thumb tip.

open.q: The radial bursa is the synovial sheath of the tendon of which muscle?

questions.q: How many synovial compartments does the extensor retinaculum create for the extensor tendons at the wrist?
questions.explain: The retinaculum is divided into six compartments. The first holds abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis.

open.q: How many synovial compartments does the extensor retinaculum create for the extensor tendons at the wrist?

questions.q: Which tendon forms the medial (ulnar) boundary of the anatomical snuffbox?
questions.explain: The medial boundary is the tendon of extensor pollicis longus. The lateral boundary is formed by abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis.

open.q: Which tendon forms the medial (ulnar) boundary of the anatomical snuffbox?

questions.q: In which direction does the glenohumeral joint most commonly dislocate?
questions.explain: The inferior part of the capsule is weakest and has no rotator cuff support, so the head usually dislocates anteroinferiorly.

open.q: In which direction does the glenohumeral joint most commonly dislocate?

questions.q: Which structure deepens the glenoid cavity?
questions.explain: The glenoid labrum is a fibrocartilaginous rim that deepens the shallow glenoid cavity. Labral tears can cause instability.

open.q: Which fibrocartilaginous structure deepens the glenoid cavity?

questions.q: Which shoulder movement is typically the most restricted in adhesive capsulitis (frozen shoulder)?
questions.explain: The inflamed, contracted capsule limits external rotation and abduction first.

open.q: Which shoulder movement is typically the most restricted in adhesive capsulitis (frozen shoulder)?

questions.q: Which ligament is the main stabiliser that prevents upward displacement of the clavicle at the acromioclavicular joint?
questions.explain: The coracoclavicular ligament (conoid and trapezoid parts) suspends the scapula from the clavicle. When it is torn, shoulder separation results.

open.q: Which ligament is the main stabiliser that prevents upward displacement of the clavicle at the acromioclavicular joint?

questions.q: Which joint is the only skeletal articulation between the upper limb and the axial skeleton?
questions.explain: The sternoclavicular joint links the clavicle to the manubrium and first costal cartilage.

open.q: Which joint is the only skeletal articulation between the upper limb and the axial skeleton?

questions.q: A toddler cries after being lifted by the hand. The elbow is held slightly flexed and the forearm pronated. What is the most likely injury?
questions.explain: In nursemaid's elbow, the radial head slips out of the annular ligament because the ligament is weak at that age.

open.q: A toddler cries after being lifted by the hand. The elbow is held slightly flexed and the forearm pronated. What is the most likely injury?
accept: radial head subluxation through the annular ligament

questions.q: In which direction does the elbow joint most commonly dislocate?
questions.explain: Posterior dislocation is the most common. The ulnar nerve, brachial artery and median nerve may be injured.

open.q: In which direction does the elbow joint most commonly dislocate?

questions.q: Injury to which ligament produces skier's (gamekeeper's) thumb?
options: Radial collateral ligament of the wrist
Ulnar collateral ligament of the thumb MCP joint
questions.explain: Forced abduction of the thumb, for example on a ski pole, ruptures the ulnar collateral ligament of the metacarpophalangeal joint.

open.q: Injury to which ligament produces skier's (gamekeeper's) thumb?
accept: ulnar collateral ligament of the first MCP joint

questions.q: Which bone articulates with the capitulum of the humerus?
questions.explain: The radial head articulates with the capitulum, and the trochlear notch of the ulna articulates with the trochlea.

open.q: Which bone articulates with the capitulum of the humerus?

questions.q: Which carpal bone is most commonly dislocated?
questions.explain: Anterior dislocation of the lunate can compress the median nerve in the carpal tunnel.

open.q: Which carpal bone is most commonly dislocated?

questions.q: The pisiform is a sesamoid bone within the tendon of which muscle?
questions.explain: The pisiform develops in the tendon of flexor carpi ulnaris and gives attachment to abductor digiti minimi.

open.q: The pisiform is a sesamoid bone within the tendon of which muscle?

questions.q: Between which two carpal bones does the ulnar canal (Guyon's canal) lie?
options: Pisiform and the hook of the hamate
Trapezium and the hook of the hamate
questions.explain: The ulnar nerve and artery pass through Guyon's canal between the pisiform and the hook of the hamate.

open.q: Between which two carpal bones does the ulnar canal (Guyon's canal) lie?

questions.q: Which dermatome supplies the thumb?
questions.explain: C6 supplies the thumb and lateral forearm, C7 the middle finger and C8 the little finger.

open.q: Which dermatome supplies the thumb?

questions.q: Which dermatome supplies the little finger?
questions.explain: C8 supplies the little finger and the medial hand. T1 supplies the medial forearm.

open.q: Which dermatome supplies the little finger?

questions.q: Which muscles form the posterior axillary fold?
questions.explain: The posterior fold is formed by latissimus dorsi and teres major, with subscapularis in the posterior wall. Pectoralis major forms the anterior fold.

open.q: Which muscles form the posterior axillary fold?

questions.q: Which nerve pierces the coracobrachialis muscle?
questions.explain: The musculocutaneous nerve pierces coracobrachialis and then runs between biceps and brachialis.
